title: The history of large language models
tagline: From Markov counting letters in a poem in 1913 to chatbots used by hundreds of millions: a century of predicting the next word.
intro: In 1913 Andrey Markov counted which letters followed which in a Russian poem, and in 1948 Claude Shannon used such counts to generate fake English. For decades the models stayed small. Then words became vectors, attention let networks look back, and the 2017 transformer could be scaled up almost without limit, until ChatGPT put an LLM in everyone's pocket.

eras.name: Counting letters and words
eras.summary: Mathematicians count which letters and words follow which, and the first chatbot fakes a conversation with simple rules.

eras.name: Statistics and small networks
eras.summary: Translation learns from millions of example sentences, and neural networks start predicting the next word.

eras.name: Words as vectors, and attention
eras.summary: Words become points in space, networks learn to translate whole sentences, and attention lets them look back at the source.

eras.name: The transformer and scale
eras.summary: One architecture, built on attention, is scaled from millions to hundreds of billions of parameters.

eras.name: Chatbots for everyone
eras.summary: Tuned with human feedback, LLMs reach hundreds of millions of people; open models, Indian-language models and new laws follow.

events.title: Counting letters in a poem
events.text: Markov went through the first 20,000 letters of Pushkin's poem Eugene Onegin, counting how often a vowel followed a vowel or a consonant. He showed that each letter's chance depends on the one before it.
events.why: It was the first chain of probabilities built from real text: the seed of every language model.

events.title: Fake English from counts
events.where: Bell Labs, Murray Hill, United States
events.text: In the paper that founded information theory, Shannon generated text by picking each letter or word according to how often it followed the previous ones. With longer contexts, the nonsense looked more and more like English.
events.why: It is exactly the idea in chapter 1: a model that predicts the next piece from counts.

events.title: People guess the next letter
events.where: Bell Labs, Murray Hill, United States
events.text: Shannon asked people to guess a hidden text one letter at a time. From how often they guessed right, he estimated that English carries only about 1 bit of information per letter, because so much of it is predictable.
events.why: It showed how much of language can be predicted from what came before.

events.title: ELIZA, the first chatbot
events.text: ELIZA matched keywords in what you typed and replied from simple scripts, most famously as a therapist who turned your words into questions. It learned nothing. Yet many users felt understood, which alarmed its creator.
events.why: The "ELIZA effect", trusting fluent text too much, is still the key caution with LLMs.

events.title: Weighing words by how rare they are
events.text: Spärck Jones proposed giving rare words more weight than common ones when matching documents to a search, an idea now called inverse document frequency.
events.why: Her statistical view of words underpins search engines and fed into later word vectors.

events.title: Translation learned from examples
events.who: Peter Brown, Robert Mercer and colleagues at IBM
events.text: IBM's team translated French to English using statistics learned from Canadian parliament records in both languages, with no hand-written grammar. A language model scored how natural each English sentence was.
events.why: Statistical translation proved that learning from lots of text could beat rules.

events.title: Networks with a longer memory
events.text: The long short-term memory (LSTM) network added gates that let a network keep information over many steps. Two decades later, LSTMs powered speech recognition and translation on phones.
events.why: It let networks read sequences, the job transformers later took over.

events.title: A neural network predicts the next word
events.text: Bengio's team trained a neural network to predict the next word, learning a vector for every word along the way. Similar words got similar vectors, so the model could handle sentences it had never seen.
events.why: Next-word prediction plus learned word vectors is the recipe LLMs still follow.

events.title: Statistical translation for everyone
events.text: Google Translate launched using statistical machine translation, trained on huge collections of translated documents from the United Nations and the European Parliament. It moved to neural networks in 2016.
events.why: Millions of people began using language models every day without knowing it.

events.title: word2vec: words as points in space
events.who: Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google
events.text: word2vec learned word vectors quickly from billions of words. Famously, king − man + woman landed near queen. Later studies found such sums work less neatly than the headlines said, and that the vectors carry social biases.
events.why: Embeddings became the standard first layer of every language model.

events.title: Sequence to sequence
events.who: Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le
events.text: An LSTM read a whole sentence into one vector, and a second LSTM wrote the translation from it. It worked surprisingly well, but long sentences were hard to squeeze into one vector.
events.why: It showed that one network could learn to map any text to any text.

events.title: Attention: look back at the source
events.who: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho and Yoshua Bengio
events.text: Instead of one squeezed vector, the translator learned to look back at the most relevant source words for each word it wrote. The paper was presented at ICLR in 2015.
events.why: Attention solved the long-sentence problem and became the heart of the transformer.

events.title: Byte-pair encoding for words
events.who: Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow and Alexandra Birch
events.text: The team borrowed a 1994 compression trick, byte-pair encoding, to split rare words into common pieces for translation. Published at ACL in 2016, it became how most LLMs make their tokens.
events.why: Subword tokens let models handle any word, even ones they never saw.

events.title: "Attention Is All You Need"
events.who: Ashish Vaswani and seven co-authors at Google
events.text: The transformer dropped step-by-step reading and used only attention, so every word could look at every other word at once. It trained much faster on GPUs and beat earlier translators.
events.why: Almost every modern LLM, from GPT to Claude, Gemini and Llama, is a transformer.

events.title: Learning from human preferences
events.who: Paul Christiano, Jan Leike and colleagues
events.text: Researchers trained an agent from people's choices between pairs of short video clips, instead of a written score. This reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) later shaped chatbots.
events.why: It gave builders a way to tune models towards what people actually prefer.

events.title: GPT: pretrain, then fine-tune
events.who: Alec Radford and colleagues at OpenAI
events.text: OpenAI pretrained a 117-million-parameter transformer on books to predict the next token, then fine-tuned it for tasks. The Generative Pre-trained Transformer was born.
events.why: Pretraining on plain text, then adapting, became the standard recipe.

events.title: BERT reads in both directions
events.who: Jacob Devlin and colleagues at Google
events.text: BERT learned by filling in hidden words using the text on both sides. Fine-tuned, it topped many language tests, and Google began using it in Search in 2019.
events.why: It showed how much pretrained transformers knew about language.

events.title: GPT-2 writes convincing paragraphs
events.text: GPT-2, with 1.5 billion parameters, wrote fluent paragraphs from a one-line prompt. OpenAI first released only smaller versions, citing possible misuse, and published the full model in November 2019.
events.why: It started the public debate about what fluent machine text could be used for.

events.title: GPT-3 and learning from examples in the prompt
events.who: Tom Brown and colleagues at OpenAI
events.text: GPT-3 had 175 billion parameters and was trained on about 300 billion tokens. Given a few examples in the prompt, it could do new tasks with no extra training. The same year, OpenAI researchers reported smooth "scaling laws" for size, data and compute.
events.why: Scale itself became the strategy, and so did its cost in chips and energy.

events.title: "Stochastic parrots": the risks of scale
events.who: Emily M. Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major and Margaret Mitchell
events.text: This paper argued that ever-bigger language models carry costs: energy use, biased and hard-to-audit training data, and fluent text that people may wrongly trust. Its publication became part of a public dispute at Google.
events.why: It put bias, energy and over-trust at the centre of the debate.

events.title: Tuning models to follow instructions
events.who: Long Ouyang and colleagues at OpenAI; DeepMind's Chinchilla team
events.text: InstructGPT used human-written examples and RLHF to make GPT-3 follow instructions; people preferred a 1.3-billion-parameter tuned model to the raw 175-billion one. The same month, DeepMind's Chinchilla showed models needed far more training text, about 20 tokens per parameter.
events.why: Teaching and data, not only size, turned out to matter.

events.title: ChatGPT opens to the public
events.text: OpenAI released ChatGPT as a free research preview. It passed a million users within about five days, and was reported to reach 100 million monthly users by January 2023, one of the fastest-growing apps ever (an analyst estimate).
events.why: LLMs went from research papers to everyday tools for students, workers and families.

events.title: A crowded field
events.text: In March 2023 OpenAI released GPT-4, without disclosing its size, and Anthropic released Claude; Google launched Bard, followed by Gemini models in December. Companies began competing on reasoning, safety and cost.
events.why: The largest models also became less open about how they were built.

events.title: Open-weight models: Llama
events.text: Meta shared LLaMA's weights with researchers; they leaked online within a week. Llama 2 followed in July 2023 under a licence allowing most commercial use, and thousands of tuned versions appeared, including many for Indian languages.
events.why: Anyone with a good computer could now run, study and adapt a capable LLM.

events.title: LLMs for Indian languages
events.who: Sarvam AI, Ola Krutrim, AI4Bharat, NPCI
events.text: Sarvam AI released OpenHathi, a Hindi model built on Llama 2 with AI4Bharat at IIT Madras, and Ola announced its Krutrim models on 15 December. Earlier, in September, NPCI had announced Hello! UPI voice payments using Hindi and English language models.
events.why: India's many languages, often costly to tokenize, got models built with them in mind.

events.title: BharatGen and Sarvam-1
events.who: Department of Science and Technology, IIT Bombay; Sarvam AI
events.text: The government launched BharatGen, a publicly funded effort led by IIT Bombay to build multilingual, multimodal models for Indian languages. In October, Sarvam released Sarvam-1, a 2-billion-parameter model for 10 Indian languages and English. In April 2025 the IndiaAI Mission chose Sarvam to build a national model.
events.why: Public money and startups both began building Indian foundation models.

events.title: The EU AI Act comes into force
events.text: The world's first broad AI law entered into force, sorting AI uses by risk. Rules for general-purpose models like LLMs apply from August 2025, including transparency about training, with most other rules from August 2026.
events.why: Governments began setting binding rules for how AI is built and used.

events.title: Cheaper training, open weights
events.text: DeepSeek-V3 used a mixture of experts: 671 billion parameters in total but only 37 billion used for each token. Its report claimed a much lower training cost than rivals, and its weights were published openly.
events.why: Efficiency, not just size, became a race of its own.

events.title: Counting the energy of one prompt
events.text: Google reported that a median text prompt to its Gemini app used about 0.24 watt-hours of energy and 0.26 ml of water. Independent estimates for other models vary widely, and total AI electricity demand keeps rising.
events.why: Energy use per answer is small, but billions of answers add up.

people.name: Andrey Markov
people.note: Counted letter sequences in Eugene Onegin in 1913, founding the theory of Markov chains.

people.name: Claude Shannon
people.note: Founded information theory and generated English-like text from letter and word counts.

people.name: Joseph Weizenbaum
people.note: Built ELIZA, then spent decades warning people not to over-trust computers.

people.name: Karen Spärck Jones
people.note: Pioneered statistical ways of weighing words that still power search.

people.name: Yoshua Bengio
people.note: Built an early neural language model (2003) and co-wrote the 2014 attention paper.

people.name: Ashish Vaswani
people.note: Lead author of "Attention Is All You Need", the 2017 transformer paper, written with seven co-authors.

people.name: Timnit Gebru
people.note: Co-wrote the 2021 "Stochastic Parrots" paper on the risks of large language models.

people.name: Mitesh Khapra
people.note: A co-founder of AI4Bharat, which builds open datasets and models for Indian languages.

series.title: Parameters in notable language models (reported)
series.caption: About a thousandfold growth in five years. Some later models, like GPT-4, did not disclose their size.

points.label: DeepSeek-V3: 671 billion (37 billion active per token)

series.title: Training text for notable models (reported)
series.caption: After 2022, builders grew the training text faster than the model size.

facts: Shannon estimated that English carries only about 1 bit of information per letter, because most letters can be guessed from what came before.
Training GPT-3 took about 3.14 × 10²³ arithmetic operations, and was estimated to use about 1,287 MWh of electricity.
In UTF-8 an English letter takes 1 byte and a Devanagari letter 3, one reason Hindi can cost more tokens.
ELIZA had no understanding at all, yet its creator's secretary reportedly asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it in private.
The transformer was invented for translation, not chat.
